title: Graphs: Reachability and Fewest Hops
summary: Store a graph as an edges table and explore it breadth first with recursive queries.
intro: A graph is a set of points joined by links: airports and flights, people and friendships, pages and links. Store each link as a row, and a recursive query can walk them to find where you can go, by which route, and in how few steps.
setup:
CREATE TABLE flights (origin text, destination text);
INSERT INTO flights (origin, destination) VALUES
    ('SFO', 'SEA'),
    ('SFO', 'DEN'),
    ('SEA', 'DEN'),
    ('DEN', 'ORD'),
    ('DEN', 'JFK'),
    ('ORD', 'JFK'),
    ('JFK', 'MIA'),
    ('MIA', 'ATL'),
    ('ATL', 'DEN');

steps.title: Neighbors and reachability
steps.body:
This lesson uses one table of one-way flights. Each row is an **edge** from `origin` to `destination`, and the airports are the **nodes**. That is all a graph needs:

```sql
CREATE TABLE flights (origin text, destination text);
-- 9 rows: SFO->SEA, SFO->DEN, SEA->DEN, DEN->ORD, DEN->JFK,
--         ORD->JFK, JFK->MIA, MIA->ATL, ATL->DEN
```

A node's **neighbors** are one `WHERE` away: `SELECT destination FROM flights WHERE origin = 'SFO'`.

To find every airport you can reach, start from the neighbors and join the CTE back to `flights`, so each round flies one more leg:

```sql
WITH RECURSIVE reach(airport) AS (
    SELECT destination FROM flights WHERE origin = 'SFO'
    UNION
    SELECT f.destination
    FROM reach AS r
    JOIN flights AS f ON f.origin = r.airport
)
SELECT airport FROM reach ORDER BY airport;
```

Use `UNION` here, not `UNION ALL`. The flights DEN -> JFK -> MIA -> ATL -> DEN form a **cycle**, so with `UNION ALL` the query would fly around that loop forever. `UNION` drops every row it has already produced. Once a round finds only airports it already knows, it adds nothing and the recursion stops.

example.title: Where SFO can fly
example.prompt: List the direct flights out of SFO, then every airport you can reach from SFO with any number of flights.
example.output:
destination
-------------
 DEN
 SEA
(2 rows)

 airport
---------
 ATL
 DEN
 JFK
 MIA
 ORD
 SEA
(6 rows)
example.explanation: The first query lists SFO's neighbors: DEN and SEA. The recursive CTE starts from those two. Each round joins the airports it found to `flights` on `f.origin = r.airport` and keeps the destinations. DEN leads to JFK and ORD, JFK leads to MIA, and MIA to ATL. ATL flies back to DEN, which `UNION` already has, so that round is empty and the query ends. SFO itself is missing because no flight goes back to it.

steps.title: Paths without cycles
steps.body:
`UNION` tells you *which* airports you can reach, but not *how*. To keep the route, carry it in an array column. Start with both ends of the first flight and append one airport per round with `||`:

```sql
SELECT destination, ARRAY['SFO', destination] ...  -- starting rows
SELECT f.destination, r.path || f.destination ...   -- one more stop
```

Now every row is new, because each path is longer than the one it came from, so `UNION` can no longer end a cycle. End it yourself: only fly on when the next airport is not already in the path.

```sql
WHERE NOT (f.destination = ANY(r.path))
```

`x = ANY(array)` is true when `x` matches any item, and the parentheses make `NOT` cover the whole test. No path can visit an airport twice, so every path ends and so does the recursion. Rows can't repeat now, so use `UNION ALL` and skip the duplicate check.

To print a path, `array_to_string(path, ' -> ')` joins the items with the separator you give. PostgreSQL also has a `CYCLE` clause that tracks visited rows for you, but an array of airport codes is simpler and gives you a route to print.

example.title: Every route from SFO
example.prompt: List every route out of SFO, stop by stop, without visiting an airport twice.
example.code:
WITH RECURSIVE routes(airport, path) AS (
    SELECT destination, ARRAY['SFO', destination]
    FROM flights
    WHERE origin = 'SFO'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT f.destination, r.path || f.destination
    FROM routes AS r
    JOIN flights AS f ON f.origin = r.airport
    WHERE NOT (f.destination = ANY(r.path))
)
SELECT array_to_string(path, ' -> ') AS route
FROM routes
ORDER BY path;
example.output:
route
-----------------------------------------------
 SFO -> DEN
 SFO -> DEN -> JFK
 SFO -> DEN -> JFK -> MIA
 SFO -> DEN -> JFK -> MIA -> ATL
 SFO -> DEN -> ORD
 SFO -> DEN -> ORD -> JFK
 SFO -> DEN -> ORD -> JFK -> MIA
 SFO -> DEN -> ORD -> JFK -> MIA -> ATL
 SFO -> SEA
 SFO -> SEA -> DEN
 SFO -> SEA -> DEN -> JFK
 SFO -> SEA -> DEN -> JFK -> MIA
 SFO -> SEA -> DEN -> JFK -> MIA -> ATL
 SFO -> SEA -> DEN -> ORD
 SFO -> SEA -> DEN -> ORD -> JFK
 SFO -> SEA -> DEN -> ORD -> JFK -> MIA
 SFO -> SEA -> DEN -> ORD -> JFK -> MIA -> ATL
(17 rows)
example.explanation: Each starting row is one flight out of SFO, with a path like `{SFO,DEN}`. Every round joins the last airport to its flights and appends the destination with `r.path || f.destination`. The `WHERE NOT (f.destination = ANY(r.path))` blocks ATL -> DEN, because DEN is already on every path that reaches ATL. That is what stops the loop. `ORDER BY path` sorts the arrays item by item, so each route comes right before the longer routes that extend it.

steps.title: Fewest hops
steps.body:
Add a `hops` column that starts at 1 and grows by 1 each round, and every row records how many flights its path took:

```sql
SELECT destination, 1, ARRAY['SFO', destination] ...  -- 1 flight
SELECT f.destination, t.hops + 1, t.path || f.destination ...
```

An airport can show up on several paths with different counts. SFO reaches DEN in 1 flight, and again in 2 through SEA. To keep the fewest, group by the airport and take the smallest count:

```sql
SELECT airport, min(hops) AS fewest_hops FROM trips GROUP BY airport;
```

The CTE lists every path that never revisits an airport, and a shortest route never needs to revisit one, so `min(hops)` is the true fewest. It also matches how a recursive CTE runs: **breadth first**. Round 1 makes every 1-flight path, round 2 every 2-flight path, and so on, so the first round that reaches an airport is its fewest hops. An airport you can't reach never appears, so it gets no row at all.

Keep the path check from the previous part. The `hops` column makes every row new, so `UNION` alone would not end a cycle. On big graphs the number of paths grows fast, so a cap like `AND t.hops < 6` limits the search.

example.title: Fewest flights from SFO
example.prompt: Find the fewest flights it takes to get from SFO to every airport it can reach.
example.code:
WITH RECURSIVE trips(airport, hops, path) AS (
    SELECT destination, 1, ARRAY['SFO', destination]
    FROM flights
    WHERE origin = 'SFO'
    UNION ALL
    SELECT f.destination, t.hops + 1, t.path || f.destination
    FROM trips AS t
    JOIN flights AS f ON f.origin = t.airport
    WHERE NOT (f.destination = ANY(t.path))
)
SELECT airport, min(hops) AS fewest_hops
FROM trips
GROUP BY airport
ORDER BY fewest_hops, airport;
example.output:
airport | fewest_hops
---------+-------------
 DEN     |           1
 SEA     |           1
 JFK     |           2
 ORD     |           2
 MIA     |           3
 ATL     |           4
(6 rows)
example.explanation: The CTE lists every path out of SFO, as in the previous part, plus a `hops` count that starts at 1 and adds 1 per flight. DEN appears with 1 hop (direct) and 2 hops (through SEA), and `min(hops)` keeps 1. ORD and JFK first appear in round 2, MIA in round 3, and ATL in round 4. Grouping by `airport` gives one row per reachable airport.

recap:
- An edges table, one row per link, stores a graph. `WHERE origin = x` gives a node's neighbors.
- `WITH RECURSIVE` with `UNION` finds every reachable node. `UNION` drops repeats, which also ends cycles.
- Carry the route in an array with `path || next` and stop at `NOT (next = ANY(path))`.
- `array_to_string(path, ' -> ')` prints a path.
- A `hops` column counts edges, and `min(hops)` with `GROUP BY` gives the fewest hops. Rounds run breadth first, so the first round that reaches a node is its shortest distance.
